L I II 
Sciatic Mononeuropathy during Cardiac 
Surgery 
Philip G. McManis, Rochester, MN 
Objective. To define the risk factors for sciatic neuropathy 
during cardiac surgery. 
Background. Sciatic nerve lesions are uncommon complica- 
tions of cardiac surgery, but are painful and cause long-term dis- 
ability when they occur. Potential causative processes are 
unknown. 
Methods. Records were reviewed for the occurrence of sciatic 
neuropathy in patients undergoing cardiac surgery between 
1976 and 1991. 
Results. Six patients with sciatic neuropathy were identified. 
All were unilateral and occurred ipsilateral to a femoral artery 
thrombosis or femoral-aortic balloon pump line, and all but one 
patient had severe peripheral vascular disease or perioperative 
anoxia. 
Conclusions. The acute onset of a sciatic neuropathy at the 
time of cardiac surgery is often due to lower-limb ischemia. 
Patients with symptomatic peripheral vascular disease who 
have a balloon pump inserted into the femoral artery or who 
develop femoral artery occlusion are at greatest risk for this 
complication. 
245P 
Measuring Diabetic Neuropathy: 
Comparison of Clinical and Physiologic 
Criteria 
Eva L. Feldman, Martin Stevens, Morton Brown, and Douglas 
Greene, Ann Arbor, MI 
Objective. Examine potential correlations between the differ- 
ent measures required to classify diabetic neuropathy (DN). 
Background. To classify DN, the San Antonio Conference rec- 
ommends at least one measure from these categories: symptoms, 
clinical examination, electrodiagnosis, quantitative sensory and 
autonomic function testing. 
Methods. Thirty-one men and 25 women, ages 24-65, with 
either type I or I1 diabetes mellitus, were recruited from an out- 
patient diabetes clinic. The neuropathy status of the patients 
was unknown. All patients were administered the Neuropathy 
Symptom Profile (NSP), Neurological Disability Score (NDS), 
Quantitative Vibration Testing (VT), Autonomic Function Test- 
ing (AF), and Nerve Conductions (NC). DN was staged according 
to Dyck, Muscle Nerve 11:21-32. 
Results. Sixty-nine percent of patients had abnormal NC, 
61% abnormal NDS, 53% abnormal VT, 34% abnormal AF and 
30% abnormal NSP. Using the Dyck classification, 38% of 
patients had no DN, 39% were stage 1, 18% stage 2 and 5% 
stage 3 DN. There was a highly significant correlation between 
abnormalities of NC, NDS and VT. Abnormal AF correlated only 
with abnormal VT. There was no correlation between abnormal 
NSF and any other measure. 
Conclusions. Symptoms do not correlate with quantitative 
measurements of DN. 
Study supported by University of Michigan Diabetes 
Research and Training Center. 
246P 
Autosomal Dominant Charcot-Marie-Tooth 
(CMT) Disease Types I and II: A Clinical, 
Electrophysiological, and Genetic Study 
Pierre Bouche, M. Gugenheim, E. LeGuern, J.M. Braz de Lima, 
G. Stevanin, A. Brice, Y. Agid, and the French CMT 
Collaborative Study Group, Paris, France 
Objective. To compare clinical, electrophysiological and genet- 
ic parameters in autosomal dominant CMT disease types I and 
I1 according to sex and transmission. 
Background. Phenotypical expression variability has been 
underlined, but differences according to sex and transmission 
have not been reported. 
Methods. All at-risk individuals from 36 families were inves- 
tigated by clinical examination, nerve conduction and elec- 
tromyographic studies. Microduplication of chromosome 17~11.2

was searched in all CMT-I patients. 
Results. Thirty-seven percent of type I- and 27% of type 11- 
affected individuals were asymptomatic. All autosomal domi- 
nant type I patients (N = 85) had a chromosome 17~11.2 dupli- 
cation, and the mean median nerve conduction velocity (NCV) 
was significantly decreased when transmission was paternal. In 
type I1 (N = 44), age at onset was earlier and mean median NCV 
was lower when transmission was paternal, although disease 
progression was not significantly different. In both types, age at 
onset and severity were variable. There was no anticipation. Age 
at onset was earlier and mean median NCV was more decreased 
in male type I1 patients. 
Conclusion. This study underlines the clinical variability and 
high frequency of asymptomatic patients, and supports the exis- 
tence of imprinting in types I and I1 and a sex difference in type 
11. 
Study supported by AFM. 
24 7P 
Stiff-Man Syndrome with GAD-Like 
Immunoreactivity: Response of a Patient to 
Plasmapheresis and Immunosuppression 
H.R. Brashear and Lawrence H. Phillips 11, Charlottesville, VA 
Objective. To study immunological, clinical and electrophysio- 
logical responses to treatment of stiff-man syndrome. 
Background. Some patients with a diagnosis of stiff-man syn- 
drome have circulating autoantibodies with GAD-like 
immunoreactivity (GAD-LIR). We report our second patient with 
stiff-man syndrome, high titers of serum GAD-LIR and typical 
EMG findings who responded to treatment. 
Methods. Indirect immunofluorescence assays, clinical 
assessments, and exteroceptive reflex measurements were car- 
ried out before, during and after plasmapheresis and immuno- 
suppression with corticosteroids. 
Results. Plasmapheresis and immunosuppression resulted in 
decreased titers of GAD-LIR, marked improvement in rigidity 
and spasms, and reduced amplitude of exteroceptive reflexes. 
Although clinical and electrophysiological improvement persist- 
ed on steroids, antibody titers returned to previous levels. 
Unlike our previously reported patient (Neurology 
1992;41:1588), this woman had detectable antibody in the CSF 
and developed seizures in late life. 
Conclusions. These results further support the use of serum 
GAD-LIR and exteroceptive reflexes as markers for stiff-man 
syndrome. Our findings also suggest that serum GAD-LIR may 
identify a subset of patients responsive to treatment, that corti- 
costeroids may be efficacious even with increasing titers, and 
that CSF GAD-LIR is a risk factor for seizures.
